Eric is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Mathematics and Physical Sciences at the College of Idaho. His expertise lies in the areas of probability, statistics, and statistics education. He joined the College of Idaho faculty in 2024 after spending three years as an Assistant Professor at St. Norbert College in De Pere, Wisconsin. After earning his degree, he worked for Capital One for two years in their home loans division before enrolling in graduate school. title: Homework 1: Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
Course Toolkit
The primary tools we’ll be using in this course are Python, Positron, git, and GitHub. We will be using them throughout the course both to learn the concepts discussed in the course and to analyze real data and come to informed conclusions.






Note



Python is the programming language. Positron is the Integrated Development Environment (IDE) where we write code. Miniforge/Conda manages our Python installations and packages.








Note



Git is a version control system (like “Track Changes” but for code) and GitHub is the cloud hosting service for your Git projects.


To make versioning simpler, this homework will be completed individually. In the future, you’ll learn about collaborating on GitHub.

title: Homework 1: Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
Exploratory Data Analysis
One of the most important components of data science is exploratory data analysis. I really like the following definition, which comes from this article (though it’s probably not the original source).

Exploratory Data Analysis refers to the critical process of performing initial investigations on data so as to discover patterns, spot anomalies, to test hypotheses and to check assumptions with the help of summary statistics and graphical representations.

Before you begin your exploratory analysis, you may already have a particular question in mind. For example, you might work for an online retailer and want to develop a model to predict which purchased items will be returned. Or, you may not have a particular question in mind. Instead, you might just be asked to look at browsing data for several customers and figure out some way to increase purchases. In either case, before you construct a fancy model, you need to explore and understand your data. This is how you gain new insights and determine if an idea is worth pursuing.

title: Homework 1: Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
Setting Up Your Environment
Before we analyze data, we need to set up our computer. This process involves installing a package manager (Miniforge), creating a virtual environment, and installing the necessary libraries.

Install Miniforge
We will use Miniforge to manage our Python installation. It pre-configures conda (package manager) and mamba (a faster version of conda) with the conda-forge channel, which is the community standard.

Go to the Miniforge GitHub page.
Download the Miniforge3 installer for your operating system (Windows, macOS, or Linux).
Run the installer and follow the prompts.

Windows: Open “Miniforge Prompt” after installation to verify.
Mac/Linux: Open your terminal.

If you’re on Mac or Linux run the following in your terminal if you’re on Windows write it in the provided Miniforge Prompt:

conda config --set auto_activate_base false




Create a Conda Environment
We never want to install packages into our “base” environment. Instead, we create a specific environment for this course. Open your terminal (or Miniforge Prompt) and run:
mamba create -n math4025 python=3.14

mamba create: Command to create an environment.
-n math4025: Names the environment “math4025”.
python=3.14: Specifies the Python version.



Activate the Environment
To use the environment, you must activate it:
mamba activate math4025
You should see (math4025) appear in your prompt.


Install Packages
Now we install the tools we need for this assignment.
mamba install pandas numpy seaborn matplotlib plotnine jupyter

pandas, numpy: Data manipulation.
seaborn, matplotlib, plotnine: Data visualization.
jupyter: Required to run Notebooks.

In the future, any time you want to install a package:

Make sure your math4025 environment is activated
Install it using mamba install name-of-package

title: Homework 1: Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
Understand Your Data
Today we will be working with the TIPS data set which is in the regclass R package. I’ve saved the data as a csv and included it in the repo for this assignment. The data in the TIPS dataset is information recorded by one waiter about each tip he received over a period of a few months working in a restaurant. We would like to use this data to address the question, “What factors affect tipping behavior?”

Loading packages in Python
We will need to leverage several different python packages to analyze our data.In python you can import packages in a few ways. Consider the following ways of importing the pandas package, which is the primary package we will use to manipulate data:

import pandas will import pandas. Every time you want to use a pandas function you’ll have to prepend pandas. (e.g. pandas.read_csv())
import pandas as pd will import pandas and allow you to use the shorthand pd (e.g. pd.read_csv())
from pandas import * will import every function from pandas (e.g. read_csv()). In general, it’s not a good idea to do this as you may create unintended conflicts if multiple packages have functions with the same name.
from pandas import read_csv() will import only read_csv() (e.g. read_csv() will work but no other pandas functions will work)

Common conventions in data science:

import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from plotnint import *
# OR
import plotnine as p9

section: Using git to track your changes
text:
Using git to track your changes
There are two ways to do this. You can either do this from the Source Control extension for Positron or from the command line (I’ve outlined both below). While the Positron extension is perfectly acceptable for this class, it is probably a good idea to learn to use the command line at some point if your plan it to do more data science.

Using Source Control Extension
Click onthe Source Control extension in the left-hand panel.

Staging your changes
Before we move on ensure that you DO NOT COMMIT YOUR CHANGES WITHOUT A COMMIT MESSAGE. This will make sense in a minute, but if you see a button that says “Commit”, don’t click it until you’ve finished reading this section.
If you have made changes to your files, you should see it listed here. Clicking on these files shows you the difference between the last committed state of the document and its current state, including changes. You should see deletions in red and additions in green.
If you’re happy with these changes, we’ll prepare the changes to be pushed to your remote repository. Stage your changes by clicking the + button next to the file you want to stage. When you do this you are preparing to save these changes to your version history.


Committing changes
When you commit changes, you add the changes you’ve staged to the version history of your repository. Write a meaningful commit message (for instance, “update author name”) in the Commit message box. Finally, click Commit. Note that every commit needs to have a commit message associated with it. DO NOT CLICK COMMIT WITHOUT WRITING A COMMIT MESSAGE.
You don’t have to commit after every change, as this would get quite tedious. You should commit states that are meaningful to you for inspection, comparison, or restoration.
In the first few assignments I will nudge you when to commit and in some cases, what commit message to use. As the semester progresses we will let you make these decisions.


Pushing changes
Go to your GitHub repo and refresh the page. Uh oh! You probably don’t see that changes you’ve made yet. This is because you still need to push your changes to Github. There are a few ways to do this, if you’re new to Git raise your hand.


Using the Command Line
Eventually you’ll be better off using git from the terminal or command line:

git add files-you-want-to-stage or git add . to stage all files that have changed
git commit -m "This is your commit message"
git push to push your changes
git pull to pull changes from your remote repo




Exercise 2
When exploring a new data set, it’s important to first understand the basics. What format is our data in? What types of information are included in the data set? How many observations are there?
In the Python ecosystem, data sets are usually stored in a 2-dimensional structure called a DataFrame. The pandas library has long been the industry standard for data manipulation. You can find more the documentation here and a quick tutorial can be found here. If you’re coming from R, you may find this webpage helpful (I’ve bookmarked it). Suppose you’ve loaded a dataset using pd.read_csv() and called it df. title: Homework 1: Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
Bivariate Plots
We may also be interested in comparing variables. To do so we should consider the following scenarios:

Categorical vs. categorical: your best bet is some kind of bar chart. If you’re interested in showing proportions or rates, use a standardized bar chart, if not, use a stacked bar chart or a dodged bar chart.
Categorical vs. numerical: there are many options here. Simplest would be boxplots, but this can often obscure information. Better plots would be boxplots with a jitter plot overlay, sina plots, or violin plots. See the code below for how to implement these is matplotlib, seaborn, and plotnine.
Numerical vs. Numerical: a good ole-fashioned scatter plot.


matplotlib
matplotlib offloads a lot of the data prepartion to you so you’ll usually have to do some processing using pandas.

# Prepare data: Create a list of 'Tip' arrays, one for each 'Weekday'
days = tips['Weekday'].unique()
data_by_day = [tips[tips['Weekday'] == d]['Tip'] for d in days]

# --- Plot 1: Boxplot ---
plt.boxplot(data_by_day, tick_labels=days)
plt.title("Tips by Day of the Week")
plt.xlabel("Day of the Week")
plt.ylabel("Tips")

# --- Plot 2: Boxplot + Jitter ---
plt.boxplot(data_by_day, tick_labels=days)
# Doesn't have jitter plot so must add jitter manually
for i, d in enumerate(days):
    y = tips[tips['Weekday'] == d]['Tip']
    x = np.random.normal(i + 1, 0.04, size=len(y)) # i+1 because boxplot is 1-indexed
    plt.scatter(x, y)
plt.title("Tips by Day of the Week")
plt.xlabel("Day of the Week")
plt.ylabel("Tips")

# --- Plot 3: Violin ---
plt.violinplot(data_by_day, showmeans=False, showmedians=True)
plt.xticks(ticks=range(1, len(days) + 1), labels=days)
plt.title("Tips by Day of the Week")
plt.xlabel("Day of the Week")
plt.ylabel("Tips")

# --- Plot 4: Sina Plot Approximation ---
# Matplotlib has no native Sina plot. 
# A common approximation is a Violin plot with inner points (or a swarm plot).
# Here we just show the violin (density) with scatter overlay.
parts = plt.violinplot(data_by_day)
for pc in parts['bodies']:
    pc.set_facecolor('#D43F3A')
    pc.set_alpha(0.3)
for i, d in enumerate(days):
    y = tips[tips['Weekday'] == d]['Tip']
    x = np.random.normal(i + 1, 0.04, size=len(y))
    plt.scatter(x, y, alpha=0.6, s=10)
plt.xticks(ticks=range(1, len(days) + 1), labels=days)
plt.title("Tips by Day of the Week")
plt.xlabel("Day of the Week")
plt.ylabel("Tips")



seaborn
seaborn codee looks a lot like matplotlib but takes care of most of the processing for you. However, seaborn tends to be a slow package.

# --- Plot 1: Boxplot ---
sns.boxplot(data=tips, x='Weekday', y='Tip')
plt.title("Tips by Day of the Week")

# --- Plot 2: Boxplot + Jitter ---
sns.boxplot(data=tips, x='Weekday', y='Tip', fliersize=0) # Hide outliers
sns.stripplot(data=tips, x='Weekday', y='Tip', jitter=True, color='black', alpha=0.5)
sns.swarmplot(data=tips, x='Weekday', y='Tip', color='black', alpha=0.5)
plt.title("Tips by Day of the Week")

# --- Plot 3: Violin ---
sns.violinplot(data=tips, x='Weekday', y='Tip')
plt.title("Tips by Day of the Week")

# --- Plot 4: Sina Equivalent (Swarmplot or Violin+Strip) ---
# Seaborn uses 'swarmplot' for non-overlapping points (beeswarm style)
sns.violinplot(data=tips, x='Weekday', y='Tip', inner=None, color=".8")
sns.stripplot(data=tips, x='Weekday', y='Tip', jitter=True)
plt.title("Tips by Day of the Week")



plotnine
plotnine mimicks ggplot2 syntax (mostly). Note that you’ll have to wrap your plots in parenthesis because Python can’t follow the line breaks in the same way as R. In addition, if you want to create multiple plots in the same cell, you have two options. One option is to convert your plotnine plots into matplotlib objects using the .draw() method to convert a plotnine object into a matplotlib figure or ._draw_using_figure(fig, [ax]) to assign the plotnine object to an existing axis within a matplotlib figure. The second is to use brick from the package patchworklib which allows you to arrange figures.

# --- Plot 1: Boxplot ---
(
    ggplot(tips, aes(x='Weekday', y='Tip'))
    + geom_boxplot()
    + labs(title="Tips by Day of the Week", x="Day of the Week", y="Tips")
)

# --- Plot 2: BoxpFlot + Jitter ---
(
    ggplot(tips, aes(x='Weekday', y='Tip'))
    + geom_boxplot(outlier_shape=None) # Hide outliers so they aren't plotted twice
    + geom_jitter(width=0.2)
    + labs(title="Tips by Day of the Week", x="Day of the Week", y="Tips")
)

# --- Plot 3: Violin ---
(
    ggplot(tips, aes(x='Weekday', y='Tip'))
    + geom_violin()
    + labs(title="Tips by Day of the Week", x="Day of the Week", y="Tips")
)

# --- Plot 4: Sina ---
(
    ggplot(tips, aes(x='Weekday', y='Tip'))
    + geom_sina()
    + labs(title="Tips by Day of the Week", x="Day of the Week", y="Tips")

You should notice that while the accuracy metrics on the training data drastically improve, there is little to no difference in the metrics for the test set. This is because of a phenomenon known as overfitting. Overfitting occurs when your model starts matching the training TOO well. A good visualization of an overfit model is Figure 2 in the Wikipedia article for overfitting. As you include more variables/information in your model, your performance will ALWAYS increase on your training data. This is one of the reasons we always use holdout sets. Eventually your model will begin to over-align to the noise in your training data and the accuracy on holdout sets will be level off and in most cases begin to degrade.
When modeling there are two related trade-offs that you need to consider. The first is the trade-off between prediction accuracy and interpretability. In general, one can typically create models with better prediction accuracy by sacrificing interpretability (e.g. by including more variables in your model, transforming these variables, etc.). Another trade-off is something called the bias-variance trade-off. As we increase the complexity of a model, we allow it to account for more and more intricate patterns in our data. In theory, this allows the model to mimic more complex relationships between our predictors and our target variables, reducing bias. On the other hand, more complex models typically have more parameters which need to be estimated which require more data to estimate accurately. When you increase the complexity of a model you usually increase the variance of the estimates of model parameters and the predictions the model makes. In other words, the model will be much more sensitive to the noise in the data that you have. Bias and variance will both decrease the accuracy of your model so you should try to minimize both. However, past a certain point, it will be a trade-off between the two.

Cross-Validation Terminology

Divide training set into two sets

Analysis set (Training fold): fit the model (similar to training set)
Assessment set (Validation fold): evaluation the model (similar to test set)

title: MATH 4025: Cross Validation and Resampling
text:
K-Fold Cross-Validation (CV)


Partition your data into \(K\) randomly selected non-overlapping “folds”

Folds don’t overlap and every training observation is in one fold
Each fold contained \(1/K\) of the training data

Looping through the folds \(k = 1, \ldots, K\):

Treat fold \(k\) as the assessment set
Treat all folds except for \(k\) as the analysis set
Fit model to analysis set (use whole modeling workflow)
Compute error metrics on assessment set

After loop, you will have \(K\) copies of each error metrics
Average them together to get performance estimate
Can also look at distribution of performance metrics

Given a value for \(K\) and a test data point \(x_0\): \[P(Y=j | X=x_0)=\dfrac{1}{K} \sum_{x_i \in \mathcal{N}_0} I(y_i = j)\] where \(\mathcal{N}_0\) is the set of the \(K\) “closest” neighbors.

title: MATH 4025: Classification + Logistic Regression
text:
Logistic Regression
Consider a one-dimensional binary classification problem:

Transform the linear model \(\beta_0 + \beta_1 \ X\) so that the output is a probability
Use logistic function: \[g(t)=\dfrac{e^t}{1+e^t} \ \ \ \text{for} \ t \in \mathcal{R}\]
Then: \[p(X)=P(Y=1|X) = P(\text{Success}| X)=g\left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 \ X\right)=\dfrac{e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 \ X}}{1+e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 \ X}}\]

title: MATH 4025: Classification + Logistic Regression
text:
Other important quantities

Odds: \(\dfrac{p(x)}{1-p(x)}\)
Log-Odds (logit): \(\log\left(\dfrac{p(x)}{1-p(x)}\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \ X\)

Linear function of predictors

Suppose the probability of success is 50%, what should \(p(x)\), your odds, and your log-odds be?

title: MATH 4025: Classification + Logistic Regression

title: MATH 4025: Classification + Logistic Regression
text:
Making predictions: Theory
For balance=$700,


\(\hat{p}(X)=\dfrac{e^{\hat{\beta}_0+\hat{\beta}_1 X}}{1+e^{\hat{\beta}_0+\hat{\beta}_1 X}}=\dfrac{e^{\text{intercept} + (\text{coef} \times 700)}}{1+e^{\text{intercept} + (\text{coef} \times 700)}}\)
Using our values: Intercept \(\approx -10.20\), Coef \(\approx 0.0052\)
\[p(700) \approx \dfrac{e^{-10.20 + 3.64}}{1+e^{-10.20 + 3.64}} \approx 0.0014\]
\[\textbf{Odds}(X) = \dfrac{\hat{p}(X)}{1-\hat{p}(X)} \approx 0.0014\]
\[\textbf{Log-Odds}(X) = \approx -6.57\]

title: MATH 4025: Feature Selection
text:
What is feature selection?

How do we choose what variables to include in our model?
Up to now… we included all of them… probably not the best idea.
Advantage of linear regression: interpretability
Including every feature decreases interpretability and can increase variance.
Reasons for feature selection:

Improve model performance (reduce overfitting/variance)
Improve model interpretability
Reduce computational cost

Parsimony: simpler models are called more parsimonious.
Occam’s Razor: more parsimonious models are better than less parsimonious models, holding all else constant.

title: MATH 4025: Feature Selection

Types of feature selection

title: MATH 4025: Feature Selection
text:
Forward Selection

Start from the empty model (no predictors)
At each step, add the single feature that improves fit the most
Repeat until a stopping criterion is met (AIC, BIC, CV error, etc.)
Greedy: never removes a feature once added

title: MATH 4025: Feature Selection
text:
Backward Selection

Start from the full model (all \(p\) predictors)
At each step, remove the single least useful feature
Repeat until a stopping criterion is met
Requires \(n > p\) so the full model can be fit

title: MATH 4025: Feature Selection
text:
Forward Selection

Let \(\mathcal{M}_0\) denote the empty model.
For \(k = 0, \ldots, p-1\):

Consider all \(p - k\) models that augment the predictors in \(\mathcal{M}_k\) with one additional predictor.
Choose the best among these \(p - k\) models, and call it \(\mathcal{M}_{k+1}\).

Select a single best model from among \(\mathcal{M}_0, \ldots, \mathcal{M}_p\).


Pros: Computationally efficient (\(1 + \frac{p(p+1)}{2}\) models).
Cons: Not guaranteed to find the best possible model out of all \(2^p\) models.

title: MATH 4025: Feature Selection
text:
Backward Selection

Let \(\mathcal{M}_p\) denote the full model, which contains all \(p\) predictors.
For \(k = p, p-1, \ldots, 1\):

Consider all \(k\) models that contain all but one of the predictors in \(\mathcal{M}_k\), for a total of \(k - 1\) predictors.
Choose the best among these \(k\) models.

Select a single best model from among \(\mathcal{M}_0, \ldots, \mathcal{M}_p\) using cross-validated prediction error, \(C_p\) (AIC), BIC, or adjusted \(R^2\).


Pros: Computationally efficient.
Cons: Not guaranteed to find the best possible model. Requires \(n > p\) so that the full model \(\mathcal{M}_p\) can be fit.







Forward vs. Backward


Both fit \(1 + \frac{p(p+1)}{2}\) models — far fewer than \(2^p\). Forward works when \(n < p\); backward does not. Neither is guaranteed to find the globally best subset.

title: MATH 4025: Feature Selection
text:
Forward-Backward Selection

Also called bidirectional stepwise selection
Start from the empty model (or any starting model)
At each step, consider both adding and removing a feature
Add the feature that most improves fit if it passes an entry threshold; remove any current feature that falls below a removal threshold
More flexible than pure forward or backward — can correct earlier mistakes
Cons: Still greedy, still no guarantee of finding the best subset

title: MATH 4025: Feature Selection
text:
Best-Subset Selection

Let \(\mathcal{M}_0\) denote the empty model
For \(k = 1, 2, \ldots, p\):

Fit all \(\binom{p}{k}\) models that contain exactly \(k\) predictors.
Pick the best (according to some criterion) among these \(\binom{p}{k}\) models, and call it \(\mathcal{M}_k\).

Select a single best model from among \(\mathcal{M}_0, \ldots, \mathcal{M}_p\).

Can use cross-validated prediction error, \(C_p\) (AIC), BIC, adjusted \(R^2\) etc…



Pros: Conceptually simple, guaranteed to find the best model for training data.
Cons: Computationally infeasible for large \(p\) (need to fit \(2^p\) models). Not very popular in practice.







Quick Check


How many models must be fit when \(p = 10\)?

title: MATH 4025: Evaluating Classification Models

Classification Metrics
Many classification matrix are based on the confusion matrix:

Accuracy: proportion of your classes that are correct \[(TP + TN)/Total\]
Recall/Sensitivity: proportion of true positives correct (true positive rate) \[TP/(TP+FN)\]
Precision/Positive Predictive Value (PPV): proportion of predicted positive that are correct \[TP/(TP+FP)\]
Specificity: proportion of true negatives correct (true negative rate) \[TN/(TN+FP)\]
Negative Predictive Value (NPV): proportion of predicted negatives that are correct \[TN/(TN+FN)\]

Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC): similar to \(R^2\) but for classification \[\frac{TP\times TN - FP \times FN}{\sqrt{(TP + FP)(TP+FN)(TN+FP)(TN+FN)}}\]

Good for imbalanced data
Considers both positives and negatives

F-Measure: harmonic mean of recall and precision \[\frac{2}{recall^{-1} + precision^{-1}} = \frac{2TP}{2TP+FP+FN}\]

Focuses more on positives
bad of imbalanced data

title: MATH 4025: Evaluating Classification Models

Recap: Classification Metrics

Accuracy: Overall correctness.
Recall (Sensitivity): Ability to find all positives.
Specificity: Ability to find all negatives.
Precision (PPV): Reliability of positive predictions.
NPV: Reliability of negative predictions.
MCC: Balanced measure even for imbalanced classes.
F-Measure: Balance between Precision and Recall.

title: Intro to Machine Learning
text:
Data Generating Process
Suppose we have

Features: \(\mathbf{X}\)
Target: \(Y\)
Goal: Predict \(Y\) using \(\mathbf{X}\)



Data generating process: underlying, unseen and unknowable process that generates \(Y\) given \(\mathbf{X}\)

title: Intro to Machine Learning
text:
Population
More mathematically, the “true”/population model can be represented by
\[Y=f(\mathbf{X}) + \epsilon\]
where \(\epsilon\) is a random error term (includes measurement error, other discrepancies) independent of \(\mathbf{X}\) and has mean zero.

GOAL: Estimate \(f\)

title: Intro to Machine Learning
text:
Why Estimate \(f(\mathbf{X})\)?
We wish to know about \(f(\mathbf{X})\) for two reasons:

Prediction: make an educated guess for what \(y\) should be given a new \(x_0\): \[\hat{y}_0=\hat{f}(x_0) \
\text{or} \
\hat{y}_0=\hat{C}(x_0)\]
Inference: Understand the relationship between \(\mathbf{X}\) and \(Y\).



An ML algorithm that is developed mainly for predictive purposes is often termed as a Black Box algorithm.

title: Intro to Machine Learning
text:
Prediction
There are two types of prediction problems:

Regression (response \(Y\) is quantitative): Build a model \(\hat{Y} = \hat{f}(\mathbf{X})\)
Classification (response \(Y\) is qualitative/categorical): Build a classifier \(\hat{Y}=\hat{C}(\mathbf{X})\)



Note: a “hat”, \(\hat{\phantom{f}}\), over an object represents an estimate of that object

E.g. \(\hat{Y}\) is an estimate of \(Y\) and \(\hat{f}\) is an estimate of \(f\)

title: Intro to Machine Learning
text:
Supervised Learning: Assessing Model Performance

When we estimate \(f(\mathbf{X})\) using \(\hat{f}(\mathbf{X})\), then,

\[
\underbrace{E\left[Y-\hat{Y}\right]^2}_{Error}=E\left[f(\mathbf{X})+\epsilon - \hat{f}(\mathbf{X})\right]^2=\underbrace{E\left[f(\mathbf{X})-\hat{f}(\mathbf{X})\right]^2}_{Reducible} + \underbrace{Var(\epsilon)}_{Irreducible}
\]

\(E[Y-\hat{Y}]^2\): Expected (average) squared difference between predicted and actual (observed) response, Mean Squared Error (MSE)
Goal: find an estimate of \(f(\mathbf{X})\) to minimize the reducible error

title: Intro to Machine Learning
text:
Supervised Learning: Assessing Model Performance


Labeled training data \((x_1,y_1), (x_2, y_2), \ldots, (x_n,y_n)\)

i.e. \(n\) training observations

Fit/train a model from training data

\(\hat{y}=\hat{f}(x)\), regression
\(\hat{y}=\hat{C}(x)\), classification


Obtain estimates \(\hat{f}(x_1), \hat{f}(x_2), \ldots, \hat{f}(x_n)\) (or, \(\hat{C}(x_1), \hat{C}(x_2), \ldots, \hat{C}(x_n)\)) of training data
Compute error:

Regression \[\text{Training MSE}=\text{Average}_{Training} \left(y-\hat{f}(x)\right)^2 = \frac{1}{n} \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left(y_i-\hat{f}(x_i)\right)^2\]
Classification \[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Training Error Rate}
& = \text{Average}_{Training} \ \left[I \left(y\ne\hat{C}(x)\right) \right]
\\
&= \frac{1}{n} \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^{n} \ I\left(y_i \ne \hat{C}(x_i)\right)
\end{aligned}
\]

title: Midterm Study Guide

1. ML Terminology and Big Picture (Slides 01–02)
Key vocabulary:

\(n\): number of observations (rows)
\(p\): number of predictors/features (columns, excluding response)
\(Y\): response (output) variable
\(X = (X_1, \ldots, X_p)\): predictor variables
Supervised learning: labeled response \(Y\) is provided; goal is to predict \(Y\) from \(X\)
Unsupervised learning: no response variable; goal is to find structure in \(X\) (e.g., clustering)
Regression: \(Y\) is quantitative (continuous)
Classification: \(Y\) is categorical (discrete classes)
Inference: understand how \(X\) affects \(Y\)
Prediction: predict \(Y\) for new observations; \(f\) is a “black box”
Parametric: assumes a specific functional form for \(f\) (e.g., linear); reduces problem to estimating a fixed set of parameters
Non-parametric: makes no strong assumptions about \(f\); more flexible but requires more data

Things to watch for:

Identifying \(n\) and \(p\) correctly: \(p\) is the number of predictors, not including \(Y\)
Distinguish regression from classification by looking at whether \(Y\) is continuous or categorical
Supervised vs. unsupervised: does the data come with labels?

title: Midterm Study Guide

2. Statistical Learning and Error Decomposition (Slide 02)
Key vocabulary:

\(f(X)\): the true (unknown) function relating \(X\) to \(Y\)
\(\hat{f}(X)\): our estimated function
Reducible error: due to \(\hat{f} \neq f\); can be improved with better models/data
Irreducible error (\(\varepsilon\)): natural variability in \(Y\) not explained by any \(X\); cannot be reduced regardless of model complexity

Key formulas:
\[Y = f(X) + \varepsilon\]
\[\text{MSE} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2\]
Things to watch for:

Irreducible error is a floor on prediction error — no model can beat it
A model with training MSE = 0 does not have zero error in general; irreducible error always remains

title: Midterm Study Guide
text:
3. Bias-Variance Tradeoff (Slides 02–03)
Key vocabulary:

Bias: error from wrong assumptions in the model; high-bias models underfit
Variance: sensitivity of \(\hat{f}\) to fluctuations in training data; high-variance models overfit
Overfitting: low training error, high test error (high variance, low bias)
Underfitting: high training error, high test error (high bias, low variance)
Test MSE U-shape: as flexibility increases, test MSE first decreases then increases

Key formula (bias-variance decomposition):
\[E\left[(y_0 - \hat{f}(x_0))^2\right] = \text{Var}(\hat{f}(x_0)) + \left[\text{Bias}(\hat{f}(x_0))\right]^2 + \text{Var}(\varepsilon)\]
Things to watch for:

As flexibility increases: variance \(\uparrow\), bias \(\downarrow\)
As flexibility decreases: variance \(\downarrow\), bias \(\uparrow\)
For KNN: as \(K\) increases, the model becomes less flexible (more bias, less variance)
Low training error + high test error = overfitting (high variance)
High training error + high test error = underfitting (high bias)

title: Midterm Study Guide
text:
4. Linear Regression and Gradient Descent (Slides 03–04)
Key vocabulary:

SLR (Simple Linear Regression): one predictor, \(\hat{Y} = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 X\)
MLR (Multiple Linear Regression): multiple predictors
OLS: minimizes the Residual Sum of Squares (RSS) \(= \sum(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2\)
Coefficient interpretation (MLR): holding all other predictors constant, a one-unit increase in \(X_j\) is associated with a \(\hat{\beta}_j\)-unit change in \(\hat{Y}\)
Gradient descent: iterative optimization; update parameters by moving opposite to the gradient
Learning rate (\(\alpha\)): controls step size; too large → diverge; too small → slow convergence

Key formulas:
\[\hat{Y} = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 X_1 + \cdots + \hat{\beta}_p X_p\]
\[\theta \leftarrow \theta - \alpha \nabla_\theta J(\theta)\]
Things to watch for:

In MLR, interpret coefficients ceteris paribus (all others held constant)
Learning rate is not the number of iterations; it controls step size
Gradient descent moves opposite to the gradient to decrease the loss

title: Midterm Study Guide
text:
5. Data Splitting and Leakage (Slide 05)
Key vocabulary:

Training set: used to fit the model
Validation set: used to tune hyperparameters and make modeling decisions
Test set: held out until the very end; used once to report final performance
Information leakage: when information from the test/validation set “leaks” into the training process

Things to watch for:

The test set must never influence any modeling decision
Leakage example: fitting a scaler on all data before splitting — test statistics influence the scaler
The validation set is used for model selection; the test set is used for final evaluation

title: Midterm Study Guide
text:
6. K-Nearest Neighbors (Slides 06–07)
Key vocabulary:

KNN regression: predict \(\hat{f}(x_0)\) as the average of the \(K\) nearest neighbors’ \(Y\) values
KNN classification: predict the majority class among \(K\) nearest neighbors
Distance metric: typically Euclidean distance
\(K\) and flexibility: small \(K\) = more flexible (low bias, high variance); large \(K\) = less flexible (high bias, low variance)
Feature scaling: necessary because KNN uses distance; features on larger scales dominate

Key formula:
\[\hat{f}(x_0) = \frac{1}{K} \sum_{x_i \in \mathcal{N}_0} y_i\]
Things to watch for:

KNN is a non-parametric method — the “\(K\)” is a hyperparameter, not a model parameter
At \(K = 1\): training error = 0 (each point predicts itself), but test error is usually high
Always scale features before applying KNN

title: Midterm Study Guide
text:
7. Preprocessing and Pipelines (Slides 07, 12)
Key vocabulary:

StandardScaler: standardizes to mean 0, std 1: \(z = (x - \bar{x}) / s\)
OneHotEncoder: converts categorical variable with \(c\) categories to \(c\) (or \(c-1\) with drop="first") binary columns
OrdinalEncoder: encodes ordered categories as integers
RareLabelEncoder: groups infrequent categories into an “Other” or “Rare” category
ColumnTransformer: applies different transformers to different columns
Pipeline: chains preprocessing steps and model in sequence; prevents leakage when used with CV
Box-Cox: power transform for positive, skewed features; parameterized by \(\lambda\)
Yeo-Johnson: like Box-Cox but handles zero/negative values

Key formula (StandardScaler):
\[z = \frac{x - \bar{x}}{s}\]
Key formula (Box-Cox):
\[x^{(\lambda)} = \begin{cases} \frac{x^\lambda - 1}{\lambda} & \lambda \neq 0 \\ \ln(x) & \lambda = 0 \end{cases}\]
Things to watch for:

The correct workflow: fit all transformers on training data only; transform both train and test using training statistics
drop="first" in OneHotEncoder: a \(c\)-category variable creates \(c-1\) columns
Pipeline + cross-validation: each fold fits transformers on the analysis set only

title: Midterm Study Guide
text:
8. Logistic Regression (Slide 08)
Key vocabulary:

Logistic function (sigmoid): maps any real number to \((0,1)\), interpreted as probability
Log-odds (logit): \(\log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right)\); logistic regression is linear in the log-odds
Odds: \(\frac{p(X)}{1 - p(X)}\); \(e^{\hat{\beta}_j}\) = multiplicative change in odds per unit increase in \(X_j\)

Key formulas:
\[p(X) = \frac{e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 X}}{1 + e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 X}}\]
\[\log\!\left(\frac{p(X)}{1 - p(X)}\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X\]
Things to watch for:

\(p(X)\) is a probability (between 0 and 1), not a class label
Logistic regression models log-odds as a linear function of \(X\); the probability itself is nonlinear in \(X\)
The default threshold of 0.5 is not always optimal

title: Midterm Study Guide
text:
9. Classification Metrics (Slide 09)
Confusion matrix:




Predicted Positive
Predicted Negative




Actually Positive
TP
FN


Actually Negative
FP
TN



Key formulas:
\[\text{Accuracy} = \frac{TP + TN}{TP + FP + FN + TN}\]
\[\text{Recall (Sensitivity, TPR)} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN}\]
\[\text{Precision (PPV)} = \frac{TP}{TP + FP}\]
\[\text{Specificity (TNR)} = \frac{TN}{TN + FP}\]
\[\text{F1} = \frac{2 \cdot \text{Precision} \cdot \text{Recall}}{\text{Precision} + \text{Recall}}\]
When to prioritize which metric:

Recall: when missing a positive is costly (e.g., cancer screening)
Precision: when false alarms are costly (e.g., invasive surgery)
Accuracy: misleading when classes are imbalanced
F1: balances precision and recall

title: Midterm Study Guide
text:
10. ROC Curve and AUC (Slide 10)
Key vocabulary:

ROC curve: plots TPR (sensitivity) on \(y\)-axis vs. FPR (\(1 -\) specificity) on \(x\)-axis, across all thresholds
AUC: area under ROC curve; ranges from 0.5 (random) to 1.0 (perfect)
Threshold: value above which a predicted probability is classified as positive

Things to watch for:

AUC = 0.5 → classifier performs no better than random guessing
AUC = 1.0 → perfect separation
Lowering threshold: TPR increases, FPR increases (more positives predicted → more TP and more FP)
AUC summarizes performance across all thresholds; a higher AUC does not guarantee better performance at any specific threshold

title: Midterm Study Guide
text:
11. Cross-Validation (Slide 11)
Key vocabulary:

K-Fold CV: split data into \(K\) folds; each fold serves as assessment set once
LOOCV: \(K = n\); each observation is the assessment set once
Analysis set: the \(K-1\) folds used to fit the model
Assessment set: the held-out fold used to evaluate
CV estimate of test error: average of \(K\) assessment-set errors

Things to watch for:

K-Fold CV: each observation appears in the assessment set exactly once
With \(n\) observations and \(K\) folds: each assessment fold has \(n/K\) observations
LOOCV has low bias but high variance and is computationally expensive
K-Fold (typically \(K = 5\) or \(K = 10\)) is often preferred in practice

title: Midterm Study Guide
text:
12. Missing Data (Slide 13)
Key vocabulary:

MCAR (Missing Completely At Random): probability of missingness is unrelated to any variable — the data are a random subsample of the complete data. Easiest to handle.
MAR (Missing At Random): probability of missingness depends on observed variables, not on the missing value itself.
MNAR (Missing Not At Random): probability of missingness depends on the unobserved (missing) value itself. Hardest to handle.
Structurally Missing: missing by design (e.g., a follow-up question that doesn’t apply).
Imputation strategies: mean/median/mode imputation; KNN imputation; model-based imputation; multiple imputation

Things to watch for:

MNAR is the hardest case — the missing data itself is informative
Imputation must occur inside a Pipeline to prevent leakage
Median imputation is more robust to outliers than mean imputation
Creating a missingness indicator column can help models learn that a value was missing

Today
We’ll cover some common pre-processing tasks provided by scikit-learn:

Standardization (e.g. centering and scaling)
Non-linear transformations (e.g. Box-Cox, Yeo-Johnson)
Normalization (scaling observations)
Encoding categorical variables
Generating polynomial features & discretization

title: MATH 4025: Pre-processing
text:
Reminder: Pipelines & ColumnTransformers
We use Pipelines and ColumnTransformers to bundle preprocessing and modeling steps, preventing data leakage and keeping our code organized.

Pipeline: Chains together a sequence of steps (like transformers) optionally ending with an estimator. Data flows sequentially through each step.

When to use: When you want to apply a sequence of transformations to the same variables in order.

ColumnTransformer: Applies different transformers (or pipelines) to different columns of an array or DataFrame.

When to use: When you have mixed data types (e.g., numeric vs. categorical) needing different preprocessing steps before being combined back together.

title: MATH 4025: Pre-processing
text:
Pipelines & Cross-Validation

When using pipelines with cross-validation, the pipeline is fit on the analysis set in each iteration, and then used to transform the assessment set for that iteration
This prevents data leakage from the assessment set into the analysis set

title: MATH 4025: Pre-processing
section: When is pre-processing part of the model?
text:
When is pre-processing part of the model?

Some pre-processing is done before we split our data

Idea: these steps shouldn’t be impacted by patterns in training data (e.g. removing ID variables, renaming categories, etc.)

Some pre-processing is done after we split our data

Idea: these steps should be impacted by patterns in training data (e.g. scaling, imputing missing values)
Think of these as part of the model

title: MATH 4025: Pre-processing
text:
Pre-Split Cleaning

Before you split your data: make sure data is in correct format
This may mean different things for different data sets
Common examples:

Fixing names of columns
Ensure all variable types are correct (programming language dependent)
Ensure all categorical variables are correct and in order (if applicable)
Remove any variables that are not important (or harmful) to your analysis (e.g. ID variables, variables that your model shouldn’t “see”)
Ensure missing values are coded as such (i.e. as NaN instead of 0 or -1 or “missing”)
Fill in missing values where you know what the answer should be (i.e. if a missing value really means 0 instead of missing)

title: MATH 4025: Pre-processing

Post-Split Cleaning

Many pre-processing steps should be thought of as part of your model
Think: will the result of this step change based on my training data?
Examples:

Scaling: mean and sd are computed from training data
Imputing missing values: missing values are imputed using the training data

Some steps can be part of your model in certain cases but not in others:

One-Hot-Encoding: if you want to keep all categories, this can be done before splitting (but may cause issues if a category is only present in an assessment set)
Removing variables: if you know a variable is not important, you can remove it before splitting (are you removing the variable due to patterns in the training data or subject matter expertise?)
Lumping rare categories: are you lumping the categories due to patterns in the training data or subject matter expertise?

Idea: think of CV as a way of evaluting your process more than just a single model fit

title: MATH 4025: Pre-processing
text:
Standardization

What it does: Standardizes features by to put them on the same scale, or scaling features to a specific range.
Functions:

StandardScaler: Centers and scales features to have a mean of 0 and variance of 1.
MinMaxScaler: Scales features to lie between a given minimum and maximum value (often between zero and one`). Robust to very small standard deviations and preserves zero entries in sparse data.
MaxAbsScaler: Scales each feature by its maximum absolute value. Meant for data that is already centered at zero or sparse data.
RobustScaler: Uses robust statistics (e.g., median and interquartile range) to scale features in the presence of outliers.

title: MATH 4025: Pre-processing
text:
Non-linear Transformation

What it does: Maps features to a different distribution to stabilize variance and minimize skewness.
Functions:

QuantileTransformer: Maps the data to a uniform or normal distribution using quantile information. Smooths out unusual distributions and is less influenced by outliers, but distorts correlations and distances within and across features.
PowerTransformer: Applies monotonic transformations (Yeo-Johnson or Box-Cox) to map data as close to a Gaussian distribution as possible. Useful for stabilizing variance and minimizing skewness.

title: MATH 4025: Pre-processing
text:
Box-Cox Transformation

Available via PowerTransformer(method='box-cox').
Attempts to make data more “normal” (Gaussian-like) by learning a parameter \(\lambda\).
Restriction: Can only be applied to strictly positive data (\(x_i > 0\)).
Formula: \[
x_i^{(\lambda)} =
\begin{cases}
\frac{x_i^\lambda - 1}{\lambda} & \text{if } \lambda \neq 0, \\
\ln(x_i) & \text{if } \lambda = 0.
\end{cases}
\]

title: MATH 4025: Pre-processing
text:
Yeo-Johnson Transformation

Available via PowerTransformer(method='yeo-johnson').
A more robust extension of Box-Cox that works with positive, negative, and zero values.
Formula: \[
x_i^{(\lambda)} =
\begin{cases}
\frac{(x_i + 1)^\lambda - 1}{\lambda} & \text{if } \lambda \neq 0, x_i \ge 0 \\
\ln(x_i + 1) & \text{if } \lambda = 0, x_i \ge 0 \\
-\frac{(-x_i + 1)^{2 - \lambda} - 1}{2 - \lambda} & \text{if } \lambda \neq 2, x_i < 0 \\
-\ln(-x_i + 1) & \text{if } \lambda = 2, x_i < 0
\end{cases}
\]

title: MATH 4025: Pre-processing
text:
Normalization

What it does: Scales individual observations (rows), rather than features (columns), so that they have a length (norm) of 1.
Intuition: Changes the magnitude of an observation without changing its direction in space.
Example Use-Case: Text classification. If Document A is just a longer version of Document B (same relative word frequencies, just more words), normalizing them ensures they look identical to your model.
Functions:

Normalizer: Scales individual samples to have a unit l1, l2, or max norm. Frequently used before clustering or calculating similarities between samples (like cosine similarity).

title: MATH 4025: Pre-processing
text:
Encoding Categorical Features

What it does: Converts categorical text data into numeric formats that machine learning algorithms can process. Also includes handling rare categories.
Functions:

OneHotEncoder: Creates dummy variables (one-hot encoding).
OrdinalEncoder: Assigns integer values to ordinal categories.
TargetEncoder: Supervised encoding based on the target variable.
RareLabelEncoder: Groups infrequent categories into a single label (from feature_engine package).

title: MATH 4025: Pre-processing
text:
Discretization

What it does: Partitions continuous features into discrete intervals or bins (also called quantization or binning).
Functions: KBinsDiscretizer, Binarizer.

title: MATH 4025: Pre-processing
text:
Generating Polynomial Features

What it does: Creates new features by generating polynomial and interaction terms, or generates B-spline basis functions for splines. This allows linear models to capture non-linear relationships.
Functions: PolynomialFeatures, SplineTransformer.

title: MATH 4025: Pre-processing
text:
Custom Transformers & Feature Selection

What it does: Applies user-defined functions to the data, or removes features based on specific criteria like lack of variability.
Functions:

FunctionTransformer: Wraps a custom Python function to be used in a pipeline.
VarianceThreshold: Removes features whose variance doesn’t meet a specified threshold (e.g., zero or near-zero variance features).

title: MATH 4025: Pre-processing
text:
Order of Preprocessing Step
Questions to ask:

Should this be done before or after data splitting?
If I do step_A first what is the impact on step_B? For example, do you want to encode categorical variables before or after normalizing?
What data format is required by the model I’m fitting and how will my model react to these changes?
Is this step part of my “model”? I.e. is this a decision I’m making based on the data or based on subject matter expertise?
Do I have access to my test predictors?

title: MATH 4025: Pre-processing
text:
Questions

Should I lump before or after dummy coding?
Should I dummy code before or after normalizing?
Should I lump before my initial split?
How does ordinal encoding impact linear regression vs. KNN?

title: MATH 4025: Pre-processing
text:
Recap

Preprocessing Needs: Prevent information leakage by exclusively using training data parameters.
scikit-learn Pipeline: Crucial for bundling preprocessing steps with the estimator to prevent data leakage.
Common Tasks:

Standardization: StandardScaler, MinMaxScaler, RobustScaler.
Non-linear Transformation: QuantileTransformer, PowerTransformer (Box-Cox, Yeo-Johnson).
Normalization: Normalizer (scales individual observations to unit norm).
Categorical Encoding: OneHotEncoder (dummies), OrdinalEncoder, RareLabelEncoder.
Discretization: KBinsDiscretizer, Binarizer.
Polynomial Features: PolynomialFeatures, SplineTransformer.
Custom/Feature Selection: FunctionTransformer, VarianceThreshold.

Order matters!: Be mindful of when to apply scaling vs. dummy-ing or imputation.

Statistical Learning vs Machine Learning vs Data Science

Machine learning arose as a sub-field of Artificial Intelligence which is a sub-fields of Computer Science
Statistical learning arose as a sub-field of Statistics

Multiple Linear Regression

Response: \(Y\)

\[

Classification \[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Training Error Rate}
&=\text{Average}_{Training} \ \left[I \left(y\ne\hat{C}(x)\right) \right]\\
&= \frac{1}{n} \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^{n} \ I\left(y_i \ne \hat{C}(x_i)\right)
\end{aligned}
\]

Compute test error:

Regression \[\text{Test MSE}=\text{Average}_{Test} \left(y-\hat{f}(x)\right)^2 = \frac{1}{m} \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^{m} \left(y_i^{test}-\hat{f}(x_i^{test})\right)^2\]
Classification \[\text{Test Error Rate}=\text{Average}_{Test} \ \left[I \left(y\ne\hat{C}(x)\right) \right]= \frac{1}{m} \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^{m} \ I\left(y_i^{test} \ne \hat{C}(x_i^{test})\right)\]

Model fit on training data \(\hat{f}(x)\)

\((x_0^{test}, y_0^{test})\): test observation
Bias-Variance Trade-Off (Theoretical) \[\underbrace{E\left(y_0^{test}-\hat{f}(x_0^{test})\right)^2}_{total \ error}=\underbrace{Var\left(\hat{f}(x_0^{test})\right)}_{source \ 1} + \underbrace{\left[Bias\left(\hat{f}(x_0^{test})\right)\right]^2}_{source \ 2}+\underbrace{Var(\epsilon)}_{source \ 3}\] where \(Bias\left(\hat{f}(x_0)\right)=E\left(\hat{f}(x_0)\right)-f(x_0)\)

title: MATH 427: Simple Linear Regression + Gradient Descent
text:
Gradient Descent for Linear Regression

Objective: We want to find \(\hat{\beta}_0\) and \(\hat{\beta}_1\) which minimizes
\[\begin{aligned}
MSE &= \dfrac{e^2_1+e^2_2+\ldots+e^2_n}{n}\\
&= \dfrac{(y_1 - \hat{y}_1)^2 +  (y_2 - \hat{y}_2)^2 + \ldots + (y_n - \hat{y}_n)^2}{n}
\end{aligned}\]
\[MSE = \dfrac{(y_1 - (\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 \ x_1))^2 +  (y_2 - (\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 \ x_2))^2 + \ldots + (y_n - (\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 \ x_n))^2}{n}\]
\[MSE = \displaystyle \dfrac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - (\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 \ x_i))^2 = \displaystyle \dfrac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2 = \displaystyle \dfrac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} (e_i)^2\]

title: MATH 427: Simple Linear Regression + Gradient Descent
text:
Gradient Descent for Linear Regression

To compute gradient, need partial derivatives of \(MSE\) with respect to \(\hat{\beta}_0\) and \(\hat{\beta}_1\).
\[\text{partial derivative of MSE w.r.t.} \ \hat{\beta}_0 = -\dfrac{2}{n} \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - (\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 \ x_i)) = -\dfrac{2}{n} \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \hat{y}_i)\]
\[\text{partial derivative of MSE w.r.t.} \ \hat{\beta}_1 = -\dfrac{2}{n} \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i (y_i - (\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 \ x_i)) = -\dfrac{2}{n} \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i (y_i - \hat{y}_i)\]

OLS

Ordinary Least Squares Regression:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\hat{\beta} =\underset{\hat{\beta}_0,\ldots, \hat{\beta}_p}{\operatorname{argmin}}SSE(\hat{\beta}) &= \underset{\hat{\beta}_0,\ldots, \hat{\beta}_p}{\operatorname{argmin}}\sum_{j=1}^n(y_j-\hat{y}_j)^2\\
&=\underset{\hat{\beta}_0,\ldots, \hat{\beta}_p}{\operatorname{argmin}}\sum_{j=1}^n(y_j-\hat{\beta}_0-\hat{\beta}_1x_{1j} - \cdots - \hat{\beta}_px_{pj})^2
\end{aligned}
\]

\(\hat{\beta} = (\hat{\beta}_0,\ldots, \hat{\beta}_p)\) is the vector of all my coefficients
\(\operatorname{argmin}\) is a function (operator) that returns the arguments that minimize the quantity it’s being applied to

title: MATH 4025: Regularization
text:
Ridge Regression
\[
\begin{aligned}
\hat{\beta} &=\underset{\hat{\beta}_0,\ldots, \hat{\beta}_p}{\operatorname{argmin}} \left(SSE(\hat{\beta}) + \lambda\|\hat{\beta}\|_2^2\right) \\
&= \underset{\hat{\beta}_0,\ldots, \hat{\beta}_p}{\operatorname{argmin}}\left(\sum_{j=1}^n(y_j-\hat{y}_j)^2 + \lambda\sum_{i=1}^p \hat{\beta}_i^2\right)\\
&=\underset{\hat{\beta}_0,\ldots, \hat{\beta}_p}{\operatorname{argmin}}\left(\sum_{j=1}^n(y_j-\hat{\beta}_0-\hat{\beta}_1x_{1j} - \cdots - \hat{\beta}_px_{pj})^2 + \lambda\sum_{i=1}^p \hat{\beta}_i^2\right)
\end{aligned}
\]

\(\lambda\) (alpha in scikit-learn) is a “tuning parameter” not estimated from the data
Idea: penalize large coefficients
If we penalize large coefficients, what’s going to happen to our estimated coefficients? THEY SHRINK!
\(\|\cdot\|_2\) is called the \(L_2\)-norm

title: MATH 4025: Regularization
text:
But… but… but why?!?


Recall the Bias-Variance Trade-Off
Our reducible error can be partitioned into:

Bias: how much \(\hat{f}\) misses \(f\) by on average
Variance: how much \(\hat{f}\) moves around from sample to sample

Ridge: increase bias a little bit in exchange for large decrease in variance
As we increase \(\lambda\) do we increase or decrease the penalty for large coefficients?
As we increase \(\lambda\) do we increase or decrease the flexibility of our model?

title: MATH 4025: Regularization
text:
LASSO
\[
\begin{aligned}
\hat{\beta} &=\underset{\hat{\beta}_0,\ldots, \hat{\beta}_p}{\operatorname{argmin}} \left(SSE(\hat{\beta}) + \lambda\|\hat{\beta}\|_1\right) \\
&= \underset{\hat{\beta}_0,\ldots, \hat{\beta}_p}{\operatorname{argmin}}\left(\sum_{j=1}^n(y_j-\hat{y}_j)^2 + \lambda\sum_{i=1}^p |\hat{\beta}_i|\right)\\
&=\underset{\hat{\beta}_0,\ldots, \hat{\beta}_p}{\operatorname{argmin}}\left(\sum_{j=1}^n(y_j-\hat{\beta}_0-\hat{\beta}_1x_{1j} - \cdots - \hat{\beta}_px_{pj})^2 + \lambda\sum_{i=1}^p |\hat{\beta}_i|\right)
\end{aligned}
\]

LASSO: Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator
\(\lambda\) (alpha in scikit-learn) is a “tuning parameter”
Idea: penalize large coefficients
If we penalize large coefficients, what’s going to happen to to our estimated coefficients THEY SHRINK!
\(\|\cdot\|_1\) is called the \(L_1\)-norm

text:

title: MATH 4025: Regularization
text:
Ridge vs. LASSO


Ridge has a closed-form solution… how might we calculate it?
Ridge has some nice linear algebra properties that makes it EXTREMELY FAST to fit
LASSO has no closed-form solution… why?
LASSO coefficients estimated numerically… how?

Gradient descent works (kind of) but coordinate descent is typically better

MOST IMPORTANT PROPERTY OF LASSO: it induces sparsity while Ridge does not

title: MATH 4025: Regularization
text:
Sparsity in Applied Math

sparse typically means “most things are zero”
Example: sparse matrices are matrices where most entries are zero

for large matrices this can provide HUGE performance gains

LASSO induces sparsity by setting most of the parameter estimates to zero

this means it fits the model and does feature selection SIMULTANEOUSLY

Let’s do some board work to see why this is…

title: MATH 4025: Missing Data

Missing Data

This lecture we will primarily focus on missing values (i.e. we have observations that don’t have values for one or more variables)
Also (maybe more) important: missing data is not necessarily the same as having a missing value…
Ask yourself: Is my sample representative of the population I’m going to be applying the model to?
You could have observations which are not in your data set which create bias in your sample (Garbage in, Garbage out)

title: MATH 4025: Missing Data
text:
Missing values

Many times, you can’t just drop missing values
Even if you can, dropping observations with missing values can generate biased data/models
Sometimes missing values give you more information
MOST IMPORTANT TAKEAWAY: that data is missing in the first place, may be informative
Types of missing data:

Missing completely at random (MCAR): there is no pattern to your missing values
Missing at random (MAR): missing values are dependent on other values in the data set
Missing not at random (MNAR): missing values are dependent on the value that is missing

Structured missingness (SM): when the missingness of certain values are depends on one another, regardless of whether the missing values are MCAR, MAR, or MNAR

title: MATH 4025: Missing Data
text:
MCAR: Examples

Sensor data: occasionally sensors break so you’re missing data randomly
Survey data: sometimes people just randomly skip questions
Survey data: customers are randomly given 5 questions from a bank of 100 questions

title: MATH 4025: Missing Data
text:
MAR: Examples

Men are less likely to respond to surveys about depression
Medical study: patients who miss follow-up appointments are more likely to be young
Survey responses: ESL respondents may be more likely to skip certain questions that are difficult to interpret (only MAR if you know they are ESL)
Measure of student performance: students who score lower are more likely to skip questions

title: MATH 4025: Missing Data
text:
MNAR: Examples

Survey on income: respondent may be less likely to report their income if they are poor
Survey about political beliefs: respondent may be more likely to skip questions when their answer is perceived as undesirable
Customer satisfaction: only customers who feel strongly respond
Medical study: patients refuse to report unhealthy habits

title: MATH 4025: Missing Data
text:
Structurally Missing: Examples

Health survey: all questions related to pregnancy are left blank by males
Bank data set: combination of home, auto, and credit cards… not all customer have all three so have missing data in certain portions
Survey: many respondents may stop the survey early so all questions after a certain point are missing
Netflix: customers may only watch similar movies and TV shows

title: MATH 4025: Missing Data

Lot of complicated ways that you can read about
Can drop column if too much of the data is missing

SimpleImputer(strategy='most_frequent'): used for nominal (having no order) categorical variable

Why use a threshold other than 0.5?

Costs of different types of errors are not equal

Example: False Negative (missing a disease) is worse than False Positive (extra test)

Class imbalance

If one class is much rarer, the model might always predict the majority class at 0.5

Specific performance requirements

Need for high sensitivity (don’t miss any positives)
Need for high specificity (don’t have any false alarms)

title: Math 4025: KNN
text:
K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) Regression

Non-parametric approach
Formally: Given a value for \(K\) and a test data point \(x_0\), \[\hat{f}(x_0)=\dfrac{1}{K} \sum_{x_i \in \mathcal{N}_0} y_i=\text{Average} \ \left(y_i \ \text{for all} \ i:\ x_i \in \mathcal{N}_0\right) \] where \(\mathcal{N}_0\) is the set of the \(K\) training observations closest to \(x_0\).
Informally, average together the \(K\) “closest” observations in your training set
“Closeness”: usually use the Euclidean metric to measure distance
Euclidean distance between \(\mathbf{X}_i=(x_{i1}, x_{i2}, \ldots, x_{ip})\) and \(\mathbf{x}_j=(x_{j1}, x_{j2}, \ldots, x_{jp})\): \[||\mathbf{x}_i-\mathbf{x}_j||_2 = \sqrt{(x_{i1}-x_{j1})^2 + (x_{i2}-x_{j2})^2 + \ldots + (x_{ip}-x_{jp    })^2}\]

Tuning Parameters

Tuning Parameters or Hyperparameters are parameters that cannot (or should not) be estimated when a model is being trained
These parameters control something about the learning process and changing them will result in a different model when fit to the full training data (i.e. after cross-validation)
Frequently: tuning parameters control model complexity
Example: \(\lambda\) (or \(\alpha\) in Python) in LASSO and Ridge regression
Today: How to choose our tuning parameters?

Grid Search

Create a grid of tuning parameters and try out each combination
Types of grids:

Regular Grid: tuning parameter values are spaced deterministically using a linear or logarithmic scale and all combinations of parameters are used (mostly what you want to use in this class)
Irregular Grids: tuning parameter values are chosen stochastically

Use when you have A LOT of parameters

title: MATH 4025: Regularization & Model Tuning
text:
Grid Search in Python

Take advantage of GridSearchCV inside sklearn.model_selection.
You provide:

Your pipeline
A dictionary of parameters ending with a list of values to search (e.g. {'model__alpha': [0.1, 1.0, 10.0]})
A cross-validation strategy (e.g. KFold)



# Let's set up our Pipeline again
X_train = candy_train.drop(columns=['winpercent'])
y_train = candy_train['winpercent']

num_vars = X_train.select_dtypes(include=['float64', 'int64']).columns.tolist()
cat_vars = X_train.select_dtypes(include=['object', 'category']).columns.tolist()

preproc = ColumnTransformer([
    ('num', StandardScaler(), num_vars),
    ('cat', OneHotEncoder(drop='first', sparse_output=False), cat_vars)
])

ridge_pipe = Pipeline([('preproc', preproc), ('model', Ridge())])
lasso_pipe = Pipeline([('preproc', preproc), ('model', Lasso())])

title: MATH 4025: Regularization & Model Tuning
text:
Using Parsimony as a Tie-Breaker

Good heuristic: One-Standard Error Rule

Use resampling to estimate error metrics
Compute standard error for error metrics
Select most parsimonious model that is within one standard error of the best performance metric

title: MATH 4025: Regularization & Model Tuning
text:
Calculating One-Standard Error: Ridge
We need custom code for this in scikit-learn. We want the model with the largest \(\alpha\) (highest penalty -> most parsimonious) whose error is no more than the lowest error + 1 standard error of the lowest error.

# 1. Identify the index of the absolute minimum RMSE
best_idx = ridge_results['mean_test_score'].argmax()

# 2. Get the RMSE and the std error bounding the best model
# Ensure we divide standard deviation by sqrt(folds) to get standard error!
import math
best_rmse = -ridge_results.loc[best_idx, 'mean_test_score']
best_se = ridge_results.loc[best_idx, 'std_test_score'] / math.sqrt(candy_folds.n_splits)

# 3. Threshold we are willing to tolerate
threshold = best_rmse + best_se
print(f"Best RMSE: {best_rmse:.3f}, Threshold: {threshold:.3f}")

# 4. Filter for alphas where RMSE <= Threshold
candidates = ridge_results[ridge_results['mean_test_rmse'] <= threshold]

# 5. Pick the most parsimonious (largest alpha)
optimal_alpha_se = candidates['param_model__alpha'].max()
print(f"Optimal Alpha (1-SE Rule): {optimal_alpha_se}")

title: MATH 4025: Regularization & Model Tuning
text:
Brief Overview

Basic Idea: iteratively select parameter values to choose based on how previous ones have done.
Instead of blindly guessing every point (Grid Search), algorithm learns which parameters look most promising.
Common Frameworks:

Bayesian Search (using Gaussian Processes)
Simulated Annealing
Successive Halving

title: MATH 4025: Regularization & Model Tuning
text:
Bayesian Search: GP


Assume performance metrics follow a Gaussian process
Consider two sets of tuning parameters: \(x_1 = (\alpha_1, k_1)\) and \(x_2 = (\alpha_2, k_2)\)
Let \(Y_1\) and \(Y_2\) be random variables representing the performance metric at these \(x\)’s
Assume \(\text{Cov}(Y_1, Y_2)\) depends on how far apart \(x_1\) and \(x_2\)

Covariance should decrease the further apart \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) are

title: MATH 4025: Regularization & Model Tuning
text:
Bayesian Search: Acquisition Function


GP process gives us predicted mean and variance of performance metrics
Imagine two scenario’s:

1: Predicted mean is slightly better than current parameter choice and variance is low

Low-Risk, Low-Reward

2: Predicted mean is slightly worst than current parameter choice but variance is high

High-Risk, High-Reward


How do we balance?
Two competing goals: Exploration (go toward high variance) and Exploitation (go toward best mean)
Acquisition function: balances these two goals

title: MATH 4025: Regularization & Model Tuning
text:
Simulated Annealing


Does anyone know what annealing is in Physics/Material Science?
Start with initial parameter combination \(x_0\)(think gradient descent)
Embark on random walk… in each step \(i\)

Consider small perturbation from \(x_{i-1}\)… let’s call it \(x_{i-1}^{\epsilon}\)
Get performance for \(x_{i-1}^\epsilon\)
If performance is better set \(x_i = x_{i-1}^\epsilon\)
If performance is worse set \(x_i = x_{i-1}^\epsilon\) with probability \(\exp(-c\times D_i\times i)\)

\(c\) is user specified constant called cooling coefficient
\(D_i\) percent difference between old and new

Otherwise \(x_i = x_{i-1}\)

Idea:

start hot: likely to accept suboptimal parameter combinations and move around
cools over time: decrease number sub-optimal acceptances

title: MATH 4025: Regularization & Model Tuning
text:
Iterative Methods in Python

Standard scikit-learn does not natively include simulated annealing or bayesian search out of the box.
You must use widely adopted extensions:

scikit-optimize for BayesSearchCV (Bayesian optimization)
Optuna or Hyperopt for advanced Bayesian / Annealing workflows.

scikit-learn does provide HalvingGridSearchCV, an iterative method that randomly samples configurations, evaluates them on small amounts of data, and “halves” the candidates repeatedly until only the best remains!

Exercise 12






Question



The time to complete cross-validation can be substantially improved by using parallel processing. Below is the output for the Gemini prompt “Generate pseudo-code in Python to do cross-validation with repetition and multiple models”. Can the for-loops below be parallelized? The primary question you want to ask yourself is “Are the different iterations of my loops independent of each other?”. If there are small changes you need to make to the code to make it parallelizable, state what they are.

# Define the number of folds (k) and the number of repetitions (r)
k = 5
r = 3

# Define the list of models to evaluate
models = {
    'model1': train_model1,
    'model2': train_model2,
    'model3': train_model3
}

# Initialize a dictionary to store the performance metrics for each model
all_performance_metrics = {}

# Loop through each model
for model_name, model_func in models.items():
    # Initialize a list to store the performance metrics for this model
    model_performance_metrics = []
    
    # Loop through each repetition
    for rep in range(r):
        # Create k-fold cross-validation object for this repetition
        kf = KFold(n_splits=k, shuffle=True, random_state=rep)
        
        # Initialize a list to store the performance metrics for this repetition
        performance_metrics = []
        
        # Loop through each fold
        for train_index, val_index in kf.split(dataset):
            # Split the data
            training_set = dataset.iloc[train_index]
            validation_set = dataset.iloc[val_index]
            
            # Train the model on the training set
            model = model_func(training_set)
            
            # Evaluate the model on the validation set
            performance = evaluate_model(model, validation_set)
            
            # Store the performance metric
            performance_metrics.append(performance)
                
        # Store the performance metrics for this repetition
        model_performance_metrics.append(performance_metrics)
        
    # Store the performance metrics for this model
    all_performance_metrics[model_name] = model_performance_metrics

# Calculate the average performance metric for each model across all repetitions
average_performance = {
    name: np.mean(metrics) 
    for name, metrics in all_performance_metrics.items()
}

# Output the average performance for each model
print("Average Performance for each model:")
print(average_performance)

You will be assessed based on six components: homework, quizzes, a job application, a job interview, a midterm exam, a hack-a-thon, and a project.

Quizzes
Videos will be posted on the course website that you are expected to watch before class. There will be a short quiz at the beginning of class every Tuesday to ensure you are keeping up with the material.


Homework
Homework will be graded on a pass/fail basis and will be assessed via presentation. Assignments will be due at the beginning of class on Thursday. Students will be randomly chosen to present their solutions. Each solution will be followed by a discussion by the class on what did and didn’t go well.

Honesty Policy: If you did not complete the homework and are honest about it, you will receive 50%. If you demonstrate no understanding of the homework during presentation, you will receive a 0%.



Job Application & Job Interview
During this course you will apply to one “job”. I will generate the job advertisement including a real company and base the job description on the course content and similar job advertisements. The job application will have three components:

A cover letter.
A resume.
A portfolio.

All three of these should be tailored to the job description and the company to which you are applying. Your portfolio will consist of self-contained data analyses of your choosing. To create your portfolio, you will be required to create a website.
After you submit your job application, you will be invited to schedule a one-hour long job interview. It is your job to schedule your job interview with Dr. Friedlander. The interview will include general interview questions, questions about your portfolio, and a “case interview” portion.


Midterm Exam
There will be one midterm exam to assess your understanding of the core concepts covered in the first half of the course.


Hack-a-thon
At some point in the semester we will participate in a “Hack-a-thon” as a class. Namely, you will be given a short period of time (1-3 days) to build a model and make a set of predictions. After the competition is over, you will be required to present on your model. Part of your score will be determine by how well your model performs and extra credit will be given to the top scoring individuals.


Project
During the latter portion of the course, you will complete a final project that involves a deep exploration of a problem. More details for the final project will be provided later in the course.

Course policies

Academic honesty
TL;DR: Don’t cheat!

The job application assignments must be completed individually but you are welcome to discuss the assignment with classmates (e.g., discuss what’s the best way for approaching a problem, what functions are useful for accomplishing a particular task, etc.). However you may not directly share (i.e. via copy/paste or copying) any code or prose with anyone other than myself.
For the hack-a-thon, everyone will submit their predictions and give their own presentations. However, you are encouraged to work together. You are allowed to share code with one another. However, everyone should be able to explain what they did and everyone’s projects should be unique in some way. Point reductions will be given if two individuals submit the exact same predictions.
For the projects, collaboration within teams is not only allowed, but expected. Communication between teams at a high level is also allowed however you may not share code or components of the project across teams.
Reusing code: Unless explicitly stated otherwise, you may make use of online resources (e.g. StackOverflow) for coding examples on assignments. If you directly use code from an outside source (or use it as inspiration), you must explicitly cite where you obtained the code. Any recycled code that is discovered and is not explicitly cited will be treated as plagiarism.
Use of artificial intelligence (AI): You are allowed and even encouraged to use AI tools (such as ChatGPT, GitHub Copilot, etc.) to supplement your learning. However, strict adherence to the following is required:

You are responsible for all work that you submit.
You must be able to explain what every line of code does and explain all results that you submit.
If you cannot explain your code or results when asked, you will receive a grade of 0 for that assignment.


If you are unsure if the use of a particular resource complies with the academic honesty policy, just ask.
Regardless of course delivery format, it is the responsibility of all students to understand and follow all College of Idaho policies, including academic integrity (e.g., completing one’s own work, following proper citation of sources, adhering to guidance around group work projects, and more). Ignoring these requirements is a violation of the Honor Code.

Late Homework: Homework is pass/fail based. Assignments are due Thursday morning. If you do not complete the assignment but are honest about it, you will receive 50%. If you demonstrate no understanding during the presentation, you will receive 0%.
Quizzes & Presentations: Late quizzes and presentations will not be accepted without an excused absence.
School-Sponsored Events/Illness: If an assignment or meeting must be missed due to a school-sponsored event, you must let me know at least a week ahead of time so that we can schedule a time for you to make up the work before you leave.
